content: 1. Administering glucagon intravenously (IV) at doses greater than 1 mg may cause nausea and vomiting and is not recommended. For diagnostic procedures, patients who have been fasting should be given oral carbohydrates afterward, provided it is compatible with the diagnostic procedure. 2. Glucagon is used off-label for overdoses of beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. The loading dose is 50–150 mcg/kg IV over one minute, followed by an infusion of 3–5 mg/hr or 50–100 mcg/kg/hr IV, titrated to achieve an adequate clinical response. 3. Glucagon is indicated for severe hypoglycemic reactions in diabetic patients treated with insulin. Oral glucose or IV dextrose should be administered to replenish glycogen stores. 4. Glucagon has orphan drug designation for the treatment of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (HH). 5. Co-administration of glucagon with anticholinergic drugs (e.g., aclidinium, atropine, benztropine, dicyclomine, glycopyrrolate, hyoscyamine, ipratropium, methscopolamine, orphenadrine, propantheline, scopolamine, tiotropium, trihexyphenidyl, tropicamide, umeclidinium) increases the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions due to additive effects on the inhibition of gastrointestinal motility. These combinations should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 6. Glucagon increases the effects of atropine and warfarin. For warfarin, this effect is observed only when doses exceed 50 mg over a two-day period. Close monitoring is recommended. 7. Glucagon decreases the toxicity of beta-blockers (e.g. 8. Indomethacin decreases the effects of glucagon through an unknown mechanism. In patients taking indomethacin, glucagon may lose its ability to raise blood glucose or may even cause hypoglycemia. Close monitoring is required. 9. Glucagon decreases the effects of various forms of insulin (e.g., insulin aspart, insulin aspart protamine/insulin aspart, insulin degludec, insulin degludec/insulin aspart, insulin detemir, insulin glargine, insulin glulisine, inhaled insulin, insulin isophane human/insulin regular human, insulin lispro, insulin lispro protamine/insulin lispro, insulin NPH, insulin regular human) by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. Endogenous glucagon is a regulatory hormone that increases blood glucose levels, while exogenous glucagon is often used to treat hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes mellitus. 10. Glucagon increases the toxicity of inhaled glycopyrrolate, hyoscyamine spray, and umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol. These combinations should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. This information highlights the importance of careful monitoring and consideration of drug interactions when using glucagon in clinical practice.
